content: Fructooligosaccharides (FOS), also referred to as oligofructose or oligofructan, are a type of oligosaccharide that serve as an alternative or artificial sweetener. Their use became prominent in the 1980s as a response to consumer interest in healthier, low-calorie food options. The term oligosaccharide describes short chains of sugar molecules, and in the case of FOS, these chains are composed of fructose molecules. The prefix oligomeans few, and saccharide refers to sugar. There are two main classes of FOS that are commercially produced. The first class is derived from the degradation of inulin, a polymer of D-fructose molecules linked by β(2-1) bonds, with a terminal D-glucose linked by an α(1-2) bond. Inulin has a degree of polymerization ranging from 10 to 60. It can be enzymatically or chemically broken down into oligosaccharides with the general structures Glu-(Fru)n (GFn) and Frum (Fm), where n and m range from 1 to 7. This process also occurs naturally in various plants, particularly in Jerusalem artichokes and chicory. Commercially, this type of FOS is marketed under names such as Oligofructose (or Raftilose) by Orafti Ltd in Belgium. Other producers include Cosun in the Netherlands, which markets the product as Frutafit or Frutalose. The primary components of this class include kestose (GF2), nystose (GF3), fructosylnystose (GF4), bifurcose (GF3), inulobiose (F2), inulotriose (F3), and inulotetraose (F4). The second class of FOS is produced through the transfructosylation activity of β-fructosidase, an enzyme derived from Aspergillus niger, acting on sucrose. The resulting mixture has the general formula GFn, with n ranging from 1 to 5. Unlike inulin-derived FOS, this class contains not only β(1-2) linkages but also other types of linkages, though these are less common. This type of FOS is primarily manufactured in Japan by Meiji Seika Kaisha. Due to the specific configuration of their glycosidic bonds, FOS are resistant to hydrolysis by salivary and intestinal digestive enzymes. Instead, they are fermented by anaerobic bacteria in the colon. This property gives FOS a lower caloric value while contributing to the dietary fiber content of the diet. FOS are more soluble than inulin and are often used as additives in yogurt and other dairy products. They are particularly effective when combined with high-intensity artificial sweeteners, as they enhance the sweetness profile and reduce aftertaste. FOS can be extracted from various fruits and vegetables, including bananas, onions, chicory root, garlic, asparagus, barley, wheat, jícama, tomatoes, and leeks. Among cultivated plants, Jerusalem artichokes and yacón have the highest concentrations of FOS. FOS has been a popular dietary supplement in Japan for many years, even before the establishment of the Functionalized Food Study Committee in 1990, which began regulating functional foods. FOS is now gaining popularity in Western cultures due to its prebiotic effects. It serves as a substrate for beneficial gut microflora, promoting gastrointestinal health. Additionally, FOS has been suggested as a supplement for preventing yeast infections. Research has shown that FOS and inulin enhance calcium absorption in both animals and humans. This occurs because the fermentation of FOS by intestinal microflora lowers the pH in the gut, increasing calcium solubility and facilitating its absorption into the bloodstream. FOS can be considered a form of dietary fiber with low caloric value. Its fermentation produces gases and acids, the latter of which provide some energy to the body. However, FOS and inulin are also fermented by less beneficial bacterial species in the gut, such as Klebsiella, E. coli, and certain Clostridium species. These bacteria are primarily responsible for the production of gases, including hydrogen and carbon dioxide, following FOS ingestion. While most individuals can tolerate 5-10 grams of FOS without experiencing discomfort, some may experience gas-related symptoms with as little as 1 gram. The optimal daily dose for adults is estimated to be around 5-10 grams. In terms of regulation, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has classified FOS as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS). However, regulatory differences exist in other regions. For example, the New Zealand Food Safety Authority (NZFSA) has warned against the use of certain European infant formula brands containing FOS, as they do not comply with local regulations. While FOS has been approved in the European Union for restricted use in infant and follow-on formulas since 1999, the NZFSA has advised parents to avoid such products for infants under six months of age.
